The remote possibility of penetrating a hydrocarbon trap with subsequent uncontrolled release raises two alternatives for consideration. First, is that after the access hole penetrates the ice/water interface, a geophysical (seismic) program be undertaken with the express intention of obtaining data on the structure of the sediments in the vicinity. The energy source (sparker, air gun, or conventional explosives) would be released in the water below the ice shelf and data would be collected by arrays of geophones on the surface of the Ross Ice Shelf. It might be possible to obtain sufficient data for a reasonable interpretation of the structure but the cost would hardly justify the results. A geophysical survey was thoroughly explored with a number of geophysicists. All agreed that the data which would be obtained, would be of limited value unless a program of high magnitude were to be initiated.
The second alternative is not to proceed with the drilling into sediment and bedrock beneath the water column. In view of the unlikelihood of releasing significant quantities of hydrocarbon and the possible precautionary measures such as have been described, this alternative does not seem justified. If the first alternative is adopted, careful consideration of the impact of that program on the biota beneath the ice shelf must be given. It is likely that the impact would be very localized.
